benchmark: C4 (en) validation perplexity -- the NON-WIKITEXT-OVERLAPPING evaluation
why_this_exists: QAT here trains on a WikiText-2 TRAIN blend and is scored on WikiText-2 TEST. There is no leakage (different splits), but the training domain matches the eval domain, so a WikiText-2 win partly measures domain alignment rather than quantization quality. C4 is web text from a different distribution and nothing in the training mix comes from it, so it tests whether a WikiText-2 gain actually generalizes. Companion to results/wikitext2_perplexity.json; the two tables are deliberately kept separate.

harness.corpus_source: allenai/c4, en/c4-validation.00000-of-00008.json.gz, documents taken in file order until ~1.29 M chars (deterministic). Rebuild with: scripts/prepare_eval_data.py --datasets c4
harness.note: Corpus sized to match wikitext2_test.txt (1,290,546 chars / 583 chunks) so the two evaluations have comparable chunk counts and error-bar widths. All four rows below used this identical harness.

results.label: QAT Q2_K, CAKLD + ptq_q2k init + WikiText/Alpaca blend (the 26.95 best)
QAT Q2_K, same but Alpaca-only (--wikitext-frac 0), the 70.88 result
PTQ Q2_K (llama-quantize on the unmodified base model)

superseded_value.reason: untied build: Q2_K token_embd with a separate Q6_K output.weight

results.why_changed: PTQ involves no training; this reflects a quantization-recipe change. scripts/quantize_ptq.sh now passes --token-embedding-type f16 --output-tensor-type f16 and drops the duplicate output.weight, so the PTQ baseline carries the same F16 tied embedding as the QAT export in place of a Q2_K embedding with a separate Q6_K output head. Both 2-bit variants are now 310 tensors / 0.5960 B elements with identical tensor names, leaving quality as the variable under test. Measured 2026-08-04; the prior value describes the superseded build recorded under superseded_value.

results.label: QAT Q2_K, batch 24, wikitext-frac 0.05 + FineWeb 0.5 blend, final checkpoint (step 48828)
results.role: CURRENT BEST on C4 (and on WikiText2, see results/wikitext2_perplexity.json), replacing qat_q2k_blend (55.9509 on C4, 1.90x fp16). The ratio_to_fp16_* fields above are raw measurements against the RAW (never fine-tuned) fp16 base model -- NOT a fair ceiling, since that baseline never saw this run's training data. No 'beats fp16' or 'closes the fp16 gap' claim should be made from them; see analysis.batch24_fineweb_scaleup.fp16_ceiling_not_yet_run. The validated comparison is vs. the prior QAT recipe (qat_q2k_blend) and vs. PTQ, both apples-to-apples.

results.label: QAT Q2_K, batch 24, wikitext-frac 0.05 + FineWeb 0.5 blend, safety-net checkpoint (step 47500)
results.role: Statistically indistinguishable from qat_q2k_fineweb_final (overlapping stderr). Kept for the record; see results/wikitext2_perplexity.json's analysis.batch24_fineweb_scaleup for why this checkpoint was measured (step-20000 trough checkpoint was unrecoverable) and why the final checkpoint should be promoted instead.

analysis.headline: About half the WikiText blend's apparent advantage is domain alignment, not quantization quality. The blend-vs-Alpaca-only spread is 2.63x on WikiText-2 (26.95 vs 70.88) but only 1.31x on C4 (55.95 vs 73.03).

qat_degradation_is_larger_off_domain.note: Measured against fp16 on the same corpus, the best QAT model loses substantially more ground on C4 than on WikiText-2.
qat_degradation_is_larger_off_domain.implication: The WikiText-2 headline number overstates this checkpoint's general quality. Quote the C4 ratio alongside it, or the 2-bit cost reads as roughly half what it is off-domain.

ptq_is_the_control_that_validates_the_co.note: PTQ is never trained, so it has no domain adaptation to inflate its WikiText-2 score. Its degradation ratio is essentially unchanged across the two corpora -- 10.34x on WikiText-2 vs 9.48x on C4. (Updated 2026-08-04 for the embedding-tying fix; was 12.91x / 12.28x. The qualitative point -- near-equal ratios across corpora -- is unaffected.)
ptq_is_the_control_that_validates_the_co.why_it_matters: This rules out the alternative explanation that C4 is simply 'harder' in a way that penalizes low-bit models generally. C4 IS harder in absolute terms (fp16 goes 21.37 -> 29.46), but that difficulty affects the fp16 denominator too. Only the TRAINED models' ratios move, which localizes the effect to their training data rather than to the corpus.
ptq_is_the_control_that_validates_the_co._note_before_2026_08_04: PTQ is never trained, so it has no domain adaptation to inflate its WikiText-2 score. Its degradation ratio is essentially unchanged across the two corpora -- 12.91x on WikiText-2 vs 12.28x on C4.

the_core_project_claim_survives.note: QAT outperforms PTQ substantially off-domain. Against the current best QAT (qat_q2k_fineweb_final): 32.19 vs 279.30 on C4, an 8.68x gap, and 18.46 vs 220.93 on WikiText-2, an 11.97x gap. Updated 2026-08-04, when PTQ was re-measured following the embedding-tying change; the prior note compared the then-current best QAT of 55.95 against PTQ 361.61 for a 6.46x C4 gap.
the_core_project_claim_survives.verdict: The central claim -- 2-bit QAT preserves far more quality than 2-bit PTQ at the same bit-width -- holds on a corpus neither model was trained toward. The margin is smaller than WikiText-2 suggests but remains large and unambiguous.
the_core_project_claim_survives._note_before_2026_08_04: QAT still beats PTQ decisively off-domain: 55.95 vs 361.61, a 6.46x gap on C4 (vs 10.24x on WikiText-2).

alpaca_only_model_is_domain_neutral.note: The Alpaca-only model barely moves in absolute terms (70.88 WikiText-2 -> 73.03 C4) and actually improves relative to fp16 (3.32x -> 2.48x).
alpaca_only_model_is_domain_neutral.why: It never saw WikiText-2 train text, so it had no domain advantage to lose. Its WikiText-2 score was, in effect, already an out-of-domain measurement.

analysis.caveat_c4_and_pretraining: C4 is a common LLM pretraining corpus, so Qwen3-0.6B's base weights may well have seen C4-derived text. That affects all four rows equally (they share the same base model) and so does not bias the comparison between them, but it means C4 is 'not in the QAT fine-tuning mix', not 'never seen by the model'.

batch24_fineweb_scaleup.note: Cross-reference: full writeup and training-time-proxy-trough caveat is in results/wikitext2_perplexity.json's analysis.batch24_fineweb_scaleup. This is the C4 (held-out generalization) half of that result.
batch24_fineweb_scaleup.headline: C4 improved MORE (in relative terms) than WikiText2 did: C4 -42.4% (55.95 -> 32.25) vs WikiText2 -31.4% (26.95 -> 18.49). Since this run deliberately traded WikiText-2-specific training data (frac 0.5 -> 0.05) for general FineWeb data (frac 0 -> 0.5), a larger C4 gain than WikiText2 gain is exactly the signal that matters here: the improvement is not domain-alignment inflation (that would show up as a WikiText2-skewed gain, the opposite pattern), it is genuine generalization from more diverse training data.
batch24_fineweb_scaleup.fp16_ceiling_not_yet_run: The ratio_to_fp16_c4 / ratio_to_fp16_wikitext2 fields on the two new rows are computed against fp16_raw -- the UNMODIFIED base model, never fine-tuned on this run's Alpaca+WikiText2+FineWeb blend. That is not a fair ceiling for a 'does QAT beat/approach fp16' claim, since fp16_raw had no chance to adapt to this data at all while the QAT model trained on it for 48828 steps -- some or all of the apparent closing of the gap (down to 1.09x on C4, and the QAT model literally beating fp16_raw on WikiText2 at 0.87x) could just be a domain-adaptation effect, not evidence about the cost of 2-bit quantization specifically. A fair ceiling (fp16 fine-tuned on the identical blend, same step count) has NOT been run -- decided not to spend further GPU budget on it for now (see project decision log / conversation record). Until that ceiling exists, treat the ratio_to_fp16_* fields as raw data only, not as support for a fp16-comparison claim either way.
batch24_fineweb_scaleup.fineweb_c4_overlap_validated: Before trusting this C4 result: checked whether FineWeb (a Common Crawl derivative) and C4 (also Common Crawl derived, built entirely from the CC-MAIN-2019-18 snapshot per the FineWeb paper, arXiv:2406.17557) share content, which would mean the C4 'generalization' gain is partially the same domain-leakage problem the WikiText2/C4 split was designed to catch, just routed through FineWeb. Re-streamed the exact FineWeb slice actually consumed in training (32,236 docs, deterministic -- reproduced identically on a second re-stream) and the exact 613 C4 eval docs. Result: 0 of the 32,236 FineWeb docs came from CC-MAIN-2019-18 (our sample-10BT pull happened to span 8 other dumps, 2013-2022); 0 exact URL matches; 0 documents met FineWeb's own near-duplicate bar (word 5-gram shingle overlap >=75%) against any doc in our FineWeb pull (highest was 53.5% containment, and manual inspection of every match above 10% showed template/boilerplate overlap -- e.g. alumni-directory software templates, generic terms-of-service language -- not shared substantive content). Caveat: this checked the specific slices actually used, not the full FineWeb/C4 corpora -- full FineWeb does structurally contain C4's source snapshot, so a future run that streams a different portion of FineWeb should re-check this.
